Dear Pinecrest Insights Hiring Team,

I'm applying for the Data Analyst (New Grad, 2027) role. I'm a senior at Brookfield University studying Computer Science with a minor in Data Science, graduating in May 2027. I want to do analytics work that helps organizations understand the people they serve, and Pinecrest's work with education, healthcare and nonprofit clients is the kind of work I'd like to do.

Last summer I was a Data Analyst Intern at Brightpath Learning, an ed-tech company. I built a Tableau dashboard that the product team used to track weekly active students, lessons completed and streaks. My manager found the breakdown of streaks by grade level especially useful. I also wrote the SQL behind the dashboard. Partway through, I found that sessions were being double-counted whenever students put the app in the background. I fixed this by redefining a session as activity with gaps of less than 30 minutes, using LAG over event timestamps. That experience showed me that a dashboard is only as trustworthy as the tables under it.

Since October 2025 I've been an undergraduate research assistant in Brookfield's Social Computing Lab. I support a PhD student's interview study on how teens use online communities for mental-health support. I sent recruitment messages, ran the eligibility screener, and transcribed and de-identified 14 interviews. I also coded 6 transcripts with the team's codebook. In our inter-rater reliability check we reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.71 after one round of reconciliation. This work taught me to handle sensitive data from young people carefully and to code qualitative data in a consistent, documented way. Your role involves coding open-ended survey responses and supporting stakeholder interviews, and I'd bring those habits to both.

In a Machine Learning course project, my team of three fine-tuned a small transformer to classify sentiment in Reddit support posts. It reached a macro-F1 of 0.81, compared with 0.72 for a TF-IDF baseline. I led the error analysis, which found that the model often labeled sarcastic or dark-humor posts as negative. That was my favorite part of the project, because understanding where a model misreads people matters as much as its score.

I'd welcome the chance to grow through Pinecrest's mentorship program and to learn to present findings clearly to clients. Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,
Avery Santos

I want to understand what happens to the people on the other side of those judgments.

**New research-direction paragraph** (replaces the "tentative research direction" paragraph):

> I am interested in how automated moderation shapes what young people feel they can say when they are looking for help. Moderators of support communities face real pressures: limited volunteer time, safety risks, and platform rules. Keyword filters and auto-removal tools help them manage those pressures. I'm curious about the less visible effects of these tools on members. How do teens notice and make sense of moderation they cannot see? Do they change or soften how they describe distress in response? And what would moderation look like if it were designed around the needs of people seeking support, as well as the people doing the moderating? I would approach these questions with qualitative methods to understand members' and moderators' experiences, and with computational methods to examine where automated judgments diverge from what people mean. I hold this direction loosely. Part of why I want to do a PhD is to learn how to turn a question that has stayed with me into rigorous research.

**Statement of Interest: HCI PhD, Khoury College of Computer Sciences**

I'm a senior at Brookfield University studying Computer Science with a minor in Data Science. I started thinking about a PhD because of my work as an undergraduate research assistant in the Social Computing Lab, and because of one question from that work that I haven't been able to put down.

Since October 2025, I've helped PhD student J. Kim with an interview study about how teens use online communities for mental-health support. My part has been mostly support work. I sent recruitment messages and ran the screener, I transcribed and de-identified interviews, and I coded several transcripts with the team's codebook. I didn't design the study or lead the analysis. But doing this work meant I heard teens describe, in their own words, what these communities mean to them. Coding with J. Kim also showed me how much discussion goes into deciding what someone meant. We didn't always agree at first, and talking through those disagreements was one of my favorite parts of the project.

Through this work I started wondering about automated moderation in support communities. My first reaction was mostly discomfort, mixed with curiosity. I could see why moderators use tools like keyword filters, since they're often volunteers trying to keep people safe. But I worried that the people who need these spaces most might be the ones getting quieted. I want to find out whether teens change how they talk about bad days once they know a bot might delete their posts, and whether moderators even know that's happening. I don't know the answer, and I don't yet know how to study it well. That's a big part of why I want to do a PhD.

The question also connects to my machine learning course project. My team of three trained a classifier to label sentiment in Reddit support posts. I did the error analysis and found that the model often marked sarcastic or darkly funny posts as negative, even when people seemed to be coping or joking with each other. Error analysis was the part of the project I found most interesting. It made me want to understand where these systems misread people, not just how to improve their scores.

I've also worked as a data analyst intern at an ed-tech company, and I'm applying to analyst jobs this year. I've enjoyed that work. But I've noticed I'm most interested in questions about people that a dashboard can't answer on its own.

At Khoury, I'd like to learn how to turn a question like mine into real research: how to design a study, work with young people ethically, and combine interviews with computational methods. I'm still figuring out whether this is the question I want to spend years on. I think learning to study it carefully is the best way to find out.
